overview: A string of Pacific storms keeps the West wet this week. The first, arriving Tuesday night, brings the heaviest snow to the Sierra and western Nevada, with another wave Thursday and Friday across Utah, Wyoming and Colorado.

regions.title: Tahoe
regions.text: A strong storm arrives Tuesday night and runs through Thursday, with heavy mountain snow, strong south winds and snow levels rising to 4500 to 5500 feet Wednesday. Kirkwood leads with 48 inches, 29 of them Wednesday. The NWS is calling for more, 62 to 95 inches Wednesday through Sunday night. A Winter Storm Warning runs from Tuesday night to Friday.

regions.title: Eastern Sierra
regions.text: The same storm reaches the eastern Sierra late Tuesday night and Wednesday, with winds near 100 mph over ridges and whiteout conditions. Mammoth should see 38 inches, 19 of them Wednesday. The NWS is calling for more, 60 to 84 inches Wednesday through Sunday night. Passes may stay difficult until the storm clears Friday.

regions.title: Northern Rockies
regions.text: A cold front brings strong gusts and mountain snow to western Wyoming and Idaho, with another system Thursday into Saturday. Grand Targhee leads with 9 inches. A Winter Weather Advisory covers Tuesday night into Wednesday.

regions.title: Wasatch
regions.text: A cold front brings snow to the Wasatch Tuesday, and a larger storm Thursday into Friday pushes snow levels near 5000 feet. Powder Mountain leads with 8 inches, and the NWS is calling for more, 18 to 34 inches Wednesday night through Friday night.

regions.title: Central Rockies
regions.text: A line of rain, thunderstorms and high-elevation snow crosses the region Tuesday, with the snow mostly falling in the evening. A second system Friday into Saturday is uncertain, with models disagreeing on strength and timing. Telluride leads with 8 inches, most of it Friday.

ahead.text: The Weather Prediction Center says a Pacific trough keeps California wet and unsettled through next Tuesday, with another trough reaching the coast around Tuesday Nov 24. The Climate Prediction Center expects deep, slow troughing over the West Nov 23 to 27.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
